fecl3-0.5m.classifiedAs: Hazards of solid iron(III) chloride hexahydrate, the pure substance, from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H302: Harmful if swallowed
H315: Causes skin irritation
H318: Causes serious eye damage

note.value:
The solution on this bench is 0.5 mol/L iron(III) chloride; the statements above are the solid's. The same supplier has no sheet for this strength: its sheet for 0.1 M or less gives Warning, with H316 and H320, mild irritation of the skin and the eyes. Its two sheets for a solution call for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: its sheet for 1 M to 2.3 M, the next strength up: Warning, with H303, H316 and H319, possible harm if swallowed and serious irritation of the eyes. The eyes are to be rinsed with water for several minutes. Both sheets also ask for flushing with water at once, kept up for 15 minutes or more, without saying whether that is for the skin or for the eyes.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

naoh-1m.classifiedAs: Hazards of solid sodium hydroxide, the pure substance, from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H314: Causes severe skin burns and eye damage
H290: May be corrosive to metals

note.value:
The solution on this bench is 1 mol/L sodium hydroxide; the statements above are those of the solid it is made from. The same supplier's sheet for solutions of 0.3 M to 6.0 M, which covers this strength, keeps Danger and, under H314, says that it burns the skin severely and damages the eyes. It calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing, and its mist or spray is not breathed.

What this lab goes by: that sheet. A poison centre or a doctor is called at once. The eyes are to be rinsed with water for several minutes, contact lenses out if easily done, and the rinsing kept up; splashed clothing comes off at once and the skin is rinsed. If any is swallowed, the mouth is rinsed and no one is made to vomit.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

statements: H314: Causes severe skin burns and eye damage
H290: May be corrosive to metals

na2co3-0.5m.classifiedAs: Hazards of solid sodium carbonate (anhydrous), the pure substance, from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H303: May be harmful if swallowed
H316: Causes mild skin irritation
H319: Causes serious eye irritation

note.value:
The solution on this bench is 0.5 mol/L sodium carbonate; the statements above are those of the solid it is made from. statements: H301: Toxic if swallowed

nicl2-0.5m.classifiedAs: Hazards of solid nickel(II) chloride hexahydrate, the pure substance, from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H301+H331: Toxic if swallowed or inhaled
H315: Causes skin irritation
H317+H334: May cause an allergic skin reaction, allergy or asthma symptoms or breathing difficulties if inhaled
H341: Suspected of causing genetic defects
H350: May cause cancer
H360: May damage fertility or the unborn child
H372: Causes damage to organs through prolonged or repeated exposure

note.value:
The solution on this bench is 0.5 mol/L nickel(II) chloride, about 12 g of the hexahydrate in each 100 mL. The same supplier's one sheet for a solution stops at 3%, and still gives Danger, with H350, H360 and H372: it may cause cancer, harm fertility or an unborn child, and damage organs over long or repeated exposure. Both sheets call for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: the solid's sheet, whose statements are above, and by which this solution is handled. It asks for a fume hood or a well-ventilated room and breathing protection, and keeps splashed clothing at the workplace. Anyone exposed, or worried, calls a poison centre or a doctor, at once if any is swallowed. The eyes are to be rinsed with water for several minutes.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

bacl2-0.5m.classifiedAs: Hazards of solid barium chloride dihydrate, the pure substance, from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H301: Toxic if swallowed
H332: Harmful if inhaled

note.value:
The solution on this bench is 0.5 mol/L barium chloride. The same supplier's sheet for solutions under 1 M gives Warning, with H303 and H333: possible harm if swallowed or breathed in. Yet its section on toxicology calls barium chloride highly toxic, harming the heart, the nerves and the kidneys among other organs. It calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: the statements above, of the solid: toxic if swallowed, H301, and harmful if breathed in, H332. Its sheet asks for a hood or a well-ventilated room, and a poison centre or a doctor called at once. If any is swallowed, the mouth is rinsed first. The eyes are to be rinsed with water for several minutes; skin is washed with plenty of water.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

H302: Harmful if swallowed

H360: May damage fertility or the unborn child

nh4no3-0.5m.classifiedAs: Hazards of solid ammonium nitrate, the pure substance, from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H272: May intensify fire; oxidizer
H303: May be harmful if swallowed
H315: Causes skin irritation
H319: Causes serious eye irritation
H335: May cause respiratory irritation

note.value:
The solution on this bench is 0.5 mol/L ammonium nitrate, about 4%, at the foot of the range of the same supplier's one sheet for the solution. That sheet prints no signal word and no hazard statement, and has every laboratory chemical treated with caution all the same. It calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: the statements above, of the solid: an oxidiser, which irritates the skin, the eyes and the airways. Its sheet keeps it away from anything that burns, and asks for a hood or a well-ventilated room. Both sheets keep it from strong acids, from reducing agents, from metal powders and from organic matter. The eyes are to be rinsed with water for several minutes; skin is washed with plenty of water.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

caco3.classifiedAs: Hazards of solid calcium carbonate, the pure substance, from a supplier's safety data sheet

note.value:

What this lab goes by: that sheet, the one document read for it here. Its section on toxicology calls the powder an irritant, and it gives a limit for the dust in a workplace's air, 15 mg/m³. Powder in the eyes is to be rinsed out with water for several minutes, contact lenses out if easily done, and the rinsing kept up; on the skin it is washed off with plenty of water.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

mg.classifiedAs: Hazards of magnesium metal, as turnings or ribbon, from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H228: Flammable solid

note.value:
The magnesium on this bench is a short piece of ribbon. The supplier's sheet for the metal as turnings or ribbon gives Danger and one statement, under H228: it is a solid that burns readily. The sheet keeps it from flames, sparks, heat and hot surfaces, and from water and acids: at this bench a short piece goes into acid on purpose, as the experiment. It calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing.

What this lab goes by: that sheet, the one document read for it here. Burning magnesium is put out with dry sand or a class D extinguisher, and never with water, with which it reacts violently. The eyes are to be rinsed with water for several minutes; skin is washed with plenty of water. Its dust is irritating.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.
